113.title: Holy, holy, holy (Isaiah 6:3)
113.hook: the preface ends and heaven and earth sing the same song
113.howItsDone: At the end of the preface, the whole congregation sings or says the Sanctus, joining the seraphim's words from Isaiah with the Palm Sunday Hosanna; in many churches everyone then kneels for the Eucharistic Prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the offertory: bread and wine carried up, and a drop of water in the wine. Your line was the ordinary is carried up.

In the year King Ozias died, the prophet Isaiah says, he saw the Lord. He is in the Temple in Jerusalem, and what he sees, nobody could paint properly. The Lord, seated on a throne, high and elevated, the edge of his robe filling the whole Temple. Above him stand fiery creatures called seraphim, each with six wings: two covering the face, two covering the feet, and two to fly. They call out to each other, back and forth, so loud that the doorposts shake and the house fills with smoke. What they're calling is sung at every Mass, all over the world, today.
screen: `ISAIAH IN THE TEMPLE.` → `SERAPHIM WITH SIX WINGS.` → `THE DOORPOSTS SHAKE.`

segments.voice: Here's what they call, in the Douay-Rheims: "Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts, all the earth is full of his glory." In Latin, the first word is Sanctus, holy, and that's the name of this moment at Mass. In Hebrew, the word is kadosh, and it means more than good or pure. It means set apart. Other. Not like anything else. Some readers hear in the triple repeat Hebrew's way of saying the utmost: holy beyond all holy. Here's how the Mass gets there. After the gifts, the priest says: lift up your hearts, in Latin, Sursum corda, and the people answer that they lift them up to the Lord. Then a prayer called the preface gives thanks, and ends by joining the angels and saints in their song. The whole church sings the seraphim's words, then adds a second line, from Palm Sunday. When Jesus rode into Jerusalem, the crowds shouted, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord." With Hosanna on either side. So in one short song, the Temple vision and the Palm Sunday crowd meet. And this isn't a copy. The church isn't imitating heaven. For a moment, Catholics believe, heaven and earth are singing the same song at the same time. The same verse is at the heart of a prayer in the synagogue, the Kedushah, so Jewish neighbors sing it too. And in the book of Revelation, the creatures around the throne never stop singing it, day and night.

segments.voice: If you pray, say the word quietly three times, holy, holy, holy, with a slow breath between each, letting each one go a little deeper than the last. If you don't pray, think of something in your life that feels set apart, a place, a memory, a person, something you'd take your shoes off for. Just hold it, and let it be other.

114.title: The consecration
114.hook: the words of Jesus are spoken and Catholics believe bread and wine become his body and blood (CCC 1376)
114.tomorrow: The Great Amen and the Our Father
114.howItsDone: During the Eucharistic Prayer the priest speaks Christ's words over the bread and wine, elevates each for the people to see and genuflects; bells are often rung, and in many countries the congregation kneels throughout.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sanctus: holy, holy, holy, the seraphim's song, as heaven and earth sing together. Your line was heaven joins in.

The singing has stopped. In this church, everyone is kneeling, and even the kids have gone quiet. The priest bends over the altar, holding a thin, round piece of bread, and speaks the words Jesus said at the Last Supper. He lifts it high, above his head, so everyone can see. A small bell rings, or a set of bells. He lowers it, and genuflects. Then the same with the cup. For a few seconds, nobody in the room moves. What Catholics believe just happened has a long, strange name.
screen: `THE SINGING STOPS.` → `THE BREAD LIFTED HIGH.` → `A BELL, AND SILENCE.`

segments.voice: At the Last Supper, Luke says, Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to his friends, saying, in the Douay-Rheims: "This is my body, which is given for you. Do this for a commemoration of me." Then the cup: his blood, of the new covenant. At the consecration, the priest repeats those words, not as a story about Jesus, but in the first person, as Christ. Catholics believe that at those words, by the power of the Holy Spirit, the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ. Not a symbol, not a reminder: Christ himself, really present. The name the Church gave this is transubstantiation. Trans, across. Substance, what a thing most deeply is. The Church teaches that the substance changes completely, while everything you can see, touch or taste stays the same: it still looks like bread, and tastes like wine. No chemistry changes; in Catholic teaching, the whole reality does. That's why the bell, the kneeling, the genuflection after each elevation. Catholics often point to John's Gospel, where Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "For my flesh is meat indeed: and my blood is drink indeed." Christians understand this meal in different ways. Orthodox Christians also believe the bread and wine truly become Christ's body and blood, and usually prefer not to explain how. Lutherans believe Christ is truly present, without this Catholic explanation. Other Protestants speak of a spiritual presence, or of a memorial. For Catholics, it's the center of their worship.

segments.voice: If you're Catholic, or you'd like to, you can kneel; if not, sit with your hands open in your lap. If you pray, you can simply be present to the one who, Catholics believe, is present there.

115.title: The Great Amen and the Our Father
115.hook: the whole church says one loud Amen, then his own prayer
115.carry: so be it, all of us
115.howItsDone: At the end of the Eucharistic Prayer the priest raises the consecrated bread and chalice and the congregation responds with the Great Amen, often sung; then all stand to pray the Lord's Prayer, followed by the priest's prayer for peace and the people's closing doxology.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the consecration, and the long word transubstantiation. Your line was this is my body.

In the generations after the apostles, a Christian teacher in Rome named Justin wrote a defense of the faith addressed to the emperor. People were spreading rumors about what Christians did at their secret gatherings, and he wanted to set the record straight. So he described a Sunday. They meet, he wrote. They read from the apostles and the prophets. Someone preaches. They pray. Bread and wine and water are brought. The one presiding gives thanks at length. And then all the people present answer with one word. Justin even explains it for the emperor, because it wasn't Greek or Latin. It was Hebrew, and it meant: so be it.
screen: `JUSTIN, IN ROME.` → `A LETTER TO THE EMPEROR.` → `ALL THE PEOPLE, ONE WORD.`

segments.voice: The word is Amen, from a Hebrew root meaning firm, solid, reliable. At Mass, the long prayer over the bread and wine ends with the priest lifting both high, the bread and the cup together, and singing that through Christ, with him and in him, all glory and honor belong to the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit. In Latin, Per ipsum, et cum ipso, et in ipso. And the whole church answers: Amen. It's called the Great Amen, often sung, sometimes repeated: the people's signature on everything the priest has just prayed. Saint Jerome wrote that in Rome the Amen boomed out like thunder from heaven. Then, straight after, everyone stands and prays the Our Father together. In the Douay-Rheims it opens: "Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name." It's the prayer Jesus taught his friends, and it's here for a reason. It asks for daily bread, just before the bread is shared. It asks to forgive, just before the sign of peace. At Mass, one thing is different. After deliver us from evil, the priest keeps going with a short prayer for peace and freedom from anxiety. Then everyone ends together, giving God the kingdom, the power and the glory, now and forever. Some churches say that line straight after the prayer; at Mass, it comes here. First a whole church signs its name. Then it prays like a family.

segments.voice: Think of something you agree with deep down: a hope for someone, a thing you know is true, something good you want to happen. If you pray, say amen to it, out loud if you can, like a signature, not a murmur; if you don't, say yes to it instead, firmly. Notice the difference between agreeing and signing.

116.title: Lamb of God (Matthew 8:8)
116.hook: the bread is broken and all say Lord, I am not worthy, only say the word
116.howItsDone: After the sign of peace the priest breaks the consecrated host while the congregation sings the Agnus Dei; he then raises it with John the Baptist's words, and all respond with the centurion's words from Matthew 8:8, adapted to 'my soul shall be healed'.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Great Amen and the Our Father. Your line was so be it, all of us.

His servant was sick at home. Jesus offered to come. And this army officer, a centurion, a powerful man used to giving orders, said no. Don't come. I'm not worthy to have you under my roof. Just say the word, and he'll be healed. Jesus marveled, and said he had not found faith so great, not even in Israel. You met him back on day thirty-nine. At Mass, just before communion, Catholics say that soldier's words: an outsider's sentence, on the lips of a whole church.
screen: `THE CENTURION, DAY THIRTY-NINE.` → `I AM NOT WORTHY.` → `HIS WORDS, BEFORE COMMUNION.`

segments.voice: After the Our Father, people turn and offer each other a sign of peace, a handshake, a nod, a hug for family. Then the priest takes the large host and breaks it. That breaking is old: in the book of Acts, the first Christians gather for the breaking of bread. He drops a small piece into the chalice, bread and wine together again. And while he does, everyone sings: Agnus Dei. Lamb of God. In Latin: Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi, miserere nobis. Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us. Then again. And at the last, instead of mercy: dona nobis pacem, grant us peace. Why a lamb? Because of John the Baptist. When he saw Jesus coming toward him, he said, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who taketh away the sin of the world." Some readers hear in it the Passover lamb, whose blood marked the doors in Egypt on the night of freedom. Then the priest lifts the broken host and says John's words, and the people answer with the centurion's. In the Douay-Rheims the officer says: "Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof: but only say the word, and my servant shall be healed." At Mass, one word changes. Not my servant. My soul. Catholics say it about themselves. They hear honesty in it: nobody earns this. And hope: one word from him is enough.

segments.voice: An old instruction, credited to Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, tells people coming to communion to make the left hand a throne for the right, because the right is about to receive a king. Rest your right hand in your left, palms up and empty: nothing in them, nothing earned. If you pray, say the centurion's sentence quietly, the way Catholics do before communion; if you don't, just keep your hands open and still.

117.title: Communion and the sending
117.hook: Catholics receive; others often come forward for a blessing; then go forth, the Mass is ended
117.howItsDone: Catholics who are prepared come forward to receive communion, answering Amen to 'the Body of Christ'; in many parishes those not receiving come forward with arms crossed for a blessing; after a closing prayer and blessing, the deacon or priest dismisses the people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Agnus Dei, the Lamb of God, and the centurion's words. Your line was only say the word.

Row by row, people stand and walk up the aisle in a slow line. An old woman with a walker. A dad carrying a sleeping toddler. A teenager in a hoodie. At the front, a priest or a lay minister holds up a small white host to each person and says four words: the Body of Christ. Each one answers with one word: Amen. Mixed into the line are people who aren't receiving. They come up with their arms crossed over their chest, and the minister gives them a blessing instead. Nobody stares.
screen: `ROW BY ROW, A SLOW LINE.` → `THE BODY OF CHRIST. AMEN.` → `ARMS CROSSED, FOR A BLESSING.`

segments.voice: Communion means union, sharing together. Catholics believe they receive Christ himself, so they prepare: at peace with God, having gone to confession for any serious sin, and fasting from food for an hour before. They receive on the tongue or in the hand, and sometimes from the cup too. That Amen is a whole creed in one word: yes, this is Christ, and yes, I belong to his body, the Church. Saint Augustine told new Christians something like: receive what you are, and become what you receive. Because communion is a sign of full unity in the Church, Catholics usually ask others not to receive. It isn't meant as a judgment on anyone. So in many parishes, anyone may come forward with arms crossed for a blessing. Afterward: silence, a last prayer, a blessing. Then the deacon or priest sends everyone out. In the old Latin: Ite, missa est. Go, it is the sending. Missa became Mass, today's word. Christians have gathered for it every Sunday for nearly two thousand years, and for about sixteen hundred of them it has carried the name of its last line: you're being sent. Same root as mission. Look back over these two weeks: the entrance, through my fault, Lord have mercy, the Gloria, the readings, the Gospel and the homily, the creed and the prayers, the gifts carried up, holy, holy, holy, the consecration, the Great Amen and the Our Father, the Lamb of God, and now communion and the sending. The Mass doesn't end at the door. It's aimed at it.

Pick one person and one kind thing you could do for them before tonight, a text, a favor, a patient answer, and be specific. If you pray, ask to be sent well; if not, just make it your mission for the day.
Mass. From the Latin missa, the sending: the whole Catholic liturgy, named for the moment the people are sent out. Today's word.

118.title: How the rosary is built
118.hook: the creed, an Our Father, three Hail Marys, then five decades each on one mystery
118.howItsDone: Catholics pray the rosary alone or in groups, often daily: the sign of the cross and the Apostles' Creed on the crucifix, an Our Father, three Hail Marys and a Glory Be, then five decades, each an Our Father, ten Hail Marys and a Glory Be while meditating on one mystery, often ending with the Hail, Holy Queen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, communion and the sending, and the word Mass, from missa, the sending. Your line was the Mass is a sending.

A string of beads wrapped around a rearview mirror. Wound around a grandmother's fingers in a hospital bed. Tucked in a soldier's pocket. Dangling from a teenager's wrist. Laid in the hands of someone in a coffin. Hang around Catholics long enough and you'll see them. You met the beads back on day four. This week, i'll open the rosary up, bead by bead, and show what people are thinking about while their fingers move. It's built like a small machine for prayer. Today's word is its main part.
screen: `BEADS ON A MIRROR.` → `IN A HOSPITAL BED.` → `A SMALL MACHINE FOR PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Start at the cross that hangs from the end. Holding it, you make the sign of the cross and say the Apostles' Creed, the one from day one hundred and one. Moving up, one big bead: an Our Father. Three small beads: three Hail Marys, traditionally for faith, hope and love. Then a Glory Be. That's the doorway. Now the circle: five groups of ten small beads, each marked off by one bigger bead. Each group of ten is a decade, from the Greek and Latin for ten. For each decade, you name a mystery, a moment from the lives of Jesus and Mary, then pray one Our Father, ten Hail Marys and a Glory Be. The Hail Mary's first half is from Luke, in the Douay-Rheims: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." and "blessed is the fruit of thy womb." The second half asks Mary to pray for us, now and at the hour of our death. Catholics describe it this way: the words make a rhythm, and while the lips say the Hail Mary, the mind stays in the scene. The name rosary comes from the Latin rosarium, a rose garden: each Hail Mary like a rose, offered. There's an old story that Mary gave the rosary to Saint Dominic. Historians see it growing slowly, over a long time. Either way, in 1569 Pope Pius the Fifth wrote it down in a form close to the one prayed today.

119.title: The joyful mysteries
119.hook: annunciation, visitation, nativity, presentation, finding in the Temple (Mondays and Saturdays)
119.howItsDone: Catholics pray the joyful mysteries of the rosary on Mondays and Saturdays (and often on Sundays of Advent and Christmas), meditating in each decade on the Annunciation, the Visitation, the Nativity, the Presentation, and the Finding in the Temple.

segments.voice: Yesterday, how the rosary is built: five decades of ten. Your line was a garden of roses.

A wedding and its months of planning. A new baby in the house. A first apartment with no furniture. People call stretches like these happy, and they mean it. But ask for the stories later, and they often have fear in them too: a scare, a fight, a night without sleep. It still gets called joy. On a Monday or a Saturday, Catholics who pray the rosary walk through a stretch like that: five scenes from the start of Jesus's life, the stories from the first weeks of Camp Two. They call them the joyful mysteries. Today's word is the second half of that name.
screen: `A HAPPY STRETCH.` → `JOY, WITH FEAR IN IT.` → `FIVE SCENES, MONDAY AND SATURDAY.`

segments.voice: Mystery, in the rosary, isn't a puzzle or a crime to solve. It comes from the Greek mysterion, and in Paul's letters that's God's plan, hidden for ages and now made known: something too deep to finish thinking about, that you can keep entering. Each decade is one of these, a door into a scene. First, the Annunciation: the angel comes to Mary, and she says yes. Second, the Visitation: pregnant Mary goes to her cousin Elizabeth, and Elizabeth's baby leaps inside her. Third, the Nativity: the birth in Bethlehem, with no room at the inn. Fourth, the Presentation: Mary and Joseph bring the baby to the Temple, and old Simeon takes him in his arms, and warns Mary that a sword will pierce her soul. Fifth, the Finding in the Temple: Jesus, twelve, goes missing for three days, and his frantic parents find him among the teachers. Look at them again. A frightening angel. A pregnancy nobody expected. A baby laid in a manger. A prophecy of grief. Three days of panic over a lost child. And these are called joyful: joy sits right alongside trouble. And the rosary pictures Mary doing exactly this. After the shepherds' visit, Luke says, in the Douay-Rheims: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." That's the rosary: keeping the scenes, turning them over. This week ran from the Sanctus, the consecration, the Great Amen, the Lamb of God and the sending to the beads. The Mass is the Church's great prayer. The rosary is a pocket-sized one.
screen: `MYSTERION: HIDDEN, NOW MADE KNOWN.` · `FIVE JOYFUL SCENES.` · `FEAR INSIDE EVERY ONE.` · `MARY KEPT AND PONDERED.` · then, large: `PONDERING THEM IN HER HEART.`

segments.voice: Pick one of the five, the yes, the visit, the birth, the old man with the baby, the lost boy found, and stand in the room: what do you smell, who's afraid, where's the joy hiding? If you pray, begin a joyful decade on your fingers, Hail Mary by Hail Mary, and let the scene play. If you don't, stay inside the picture.
